metadata.title: It Talks to Claude, Not You.
metadata.subtitle: Command Development · Claude Code
metadata.purpose: Take apart the slash-command case: explain that a command's body is a prompt Claude reads, evaluate what the docs specify precisely and what they leave elsewhere, and name the design trade-off — one file, three homes, no built-in validator. Land the carry-out that a command's body is instructions Claude reads, never a message to the person running it.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> BHTF (the correct/incorrect review-command example: planted, then paid off as an LLM exercise)

beats.narration_text: You picture the body speaking to you — it's your file, in your project, your command. It isn't. The body is a prompt Claude reads. That's the whole trick, and it's why so many first commands quietly do nothing. Let me pull one apart and show you the wiring.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. One markdown file, one optional settings block on top. Three homes: project commands scoped to that one project; personal commands in your home folder, visible across every project on your machine; and plugin commands bundled inside a plugin, available the moment it installs. The settings block carries five fields — description for the help menu, allowed-tools listing what the command can call, model to pick which one runs it, argument-hint to shape autocomplete, and disable-invoke to shut off automatic triggering. They optimized for one file working in three contexts unchanged; the cost is that you have to know where to look for it.

production_viz.label: ONE FILE, THREE HOMES
production_viz.caption: lives at the top of the file — project, personal, or plugin

beats.narration_text: Here's the anchor, and it's the part everyone misses first time. A command's body is read by Claude, not shown to the person who typed it. Correct: "review this code for security issues and list each one with a line number." That's a direction Claude can act on. Incorrect: "this command will review your code and give you a report." That sentence describes what the user will see — Claude has nothing to actually do with it. Every command body should read like the first: a direction, never a description of an outcome. Get it wrong and the command runs quietly and does nothing, because you told Claude what would happen instead of what to do.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — WHO IT'S FOR
production_viz.caption: correct: 'review this code for security issues' — a direction, not a description

beats.narration_text: Now judge what the docs give you and what they don't. Fully specified: the three locations, the five settings fields, and the argument syntax — a dollar sign and number for a positional value, an at-sign for a file, an exclamation mark with backticks to run a shell command inline. That's precise. Left elsewhere: the exact bash syntax for that inline shell lives on a separate reference page, and there's no built-in validator to tell you whether a command file is well-formed before you run it. They optimized for a clean spec surface at the cost of a self-checking one — you catch mistakes at runtime, not at write-time.

production_viz.label: PRECISE HERE, LEFT ELSEWHERE
production_viz.caption: spelled out here; look elsewhere for the rest

beats.narration_text: The take-out: a Claude Code command is a markdown file. Frontmatter tells Claude when and how to run it. The body is instructions Claude reads — never a message meant for the person running it. Write for the reader who will execute your words.

props.quote: A Claude Code command is a markdown file: frontmatter tells Claude when and how to run it, and the body is instructions Claude reads — never a message meant for the person running it.
props.sparkLine: Instructions for Claude, not a message to you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm writing my first Claude Code slash command — a project command in .claude/commands/review-pr.md that reviews a pull request and posts a summary. Give me the full file: frontmatter with allowed-tools scoped to only the git and gh calls it actually needs, an argument-hint showing the PR number, and a body written as direct instructions Claude will execute — verbs, checks, expected outputs — never a description of what the user will see happen. Then explain why each frontmatter field earned its slot. Go deeper: ask the same model to write a second command whose body accidentally describes an outcome instead of giving a direction, and diff the two — where does the wrong version quietly do nothing?
